sections.h2: Should a Strongsville owner list the house or take a cash offer?
sections.html:
It comes down to timing and condition. Strongsville houses that are updated tend to suit the open market, and houses with deferred work or an estate attached may move faster to a buyer who does not ask for repairs. With 82 percent of homes owner-occupied, many sellers here are leaving a house they have kept for a long time.

  • Agent listing: exposure to Cleveland-area buyers, with inspection and appraisal hurdles still ahead.
  • Owner-run sale: no commission, but the pricing, contract and disclosure form are yours to handle.
  • As-is cash purchase: a single negotiation with no staging, and a closing date that you and the buyer agree on.

Each path finishes with a deed presented in Cleveland to the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Strongsville?
sections.html:
Strongsville is a Cleveland suburb of 24.64 square miles in Cuyahoga County. The name honors John Stoughton Strong, who brought settlers here in 1816, and the township was officially organized on February 25, 1818. Village status came in 1923, followed by city status in 1961.

The city's nickname, Crossroads of the Nation, began where a railroad met an electric line between Cleveland and Wooster. Since that line closed in 1931 the motto and seal point to Interstate 71 and the Ohio Turnpike instead. Highway access can headline a listing.

The Rocky River's east branch enters from North Royalton, and Cleveland Metroparks manage its banks as Mill Stream Run Reservation, with Bonnie Park and Ranger Lake. The Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Authority runs buses through town. Southpark Mall and the Strongsville Business and Technology Park, which Wikipedia calls the largest industrial park in Northeast Ohio, are two of its major commercial sites. History shows up in the housing stock too: the Pomeroy House, built in 1847, is a former Underground Railroad stop, and Beebetown is a historic neighborhood.

sections.h2: Who lives in Strongsville, and who buys there?
sections.html:
Strongsville's median age was 45.8 in 2020, and nearly a quarter of residents were past 65. Married couples headed 58.2 percent of its 18,643 households, and 26.0 percent lived alone. Of 19,406 housing units, 3.9 percent were empty.

That profile suggests plenty of owners who have stayed put a long time. When they downsize or an estate settles, an outdated kitchen, bath or mechanical system may be easier to sell as-is than to renovate. Buyers are well educated, with 48.3 percent of adults holding a bachelor's degree or more, and the mean commute is 25.5 minutes.

sections.h2: Which Strongsville schools and parks matter to buyers?
sections.html:
Strongsville City Schools has five elementary buildings (Chapman, Kinsner, Muraski, Surrarrer and Whitney), a middle school on Pearl Road and a high school on Lunn Road. Allen, Drake and Zellers elementary schools have closed as enrollment fell. St. Joseph and John's is a Catholic school through eighth grade.

A bond issue of $81 million passed in 2012 and paid for a combined middle school, high school renovations and technology upgrades, with the new middle school ready for 2016-2017.

  • Town Center Park, opened in 2024 with a pavilion, two playgrounds, and tennis, pickleball and volleyball courts.
  • Ehrnfelt Recreation and Senior Center, the Walter F. Ehrnfelt Covered Bridge and the Strongsville ice rink.
  • Strongsville Commons and the Clock Tower, site of the Homecoming and the Rib Burnoff.
  • Gardenview Horticultural Park and the Freedom Trail veterans memorial.

Community events cluster around the Commons and the Clock Tower: the Homecoming, the Rib Burnoff, a Winter Lighting Ceremony and, each September, the Harvest Festival at the Historical Society's village of restored buildings and a replica log cabin. A house within walking distance of Town Center Park or the Commons can use that in its description.

sections.h2: What does the Strongsville Building Department handle?
sections.html:
Permits, contractor registration, business licensing, inspections and code compliance all run through the office at 16099 Foltz Parkway. It is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., takes online submissions all day and night, and answers at 440-580-3105.

The city lists additions, decks, fences, sheds, roofs, windows and doors, pools, electrical, plumbing, HVAC and garages as permit work. A contractor has to register with Strongsville before a permit can be issued, and a homeowner permit covers only labor the owner performs. Inspections need 24 hours of notice, and voicemail requests are not accepted.

Warmer months bring property maintenance inspections, and inspectors carry a city-issued photo ID. Ask to see it, and if a notice arrives, clear the violation before listing.

sections.h2: How does a deed transfer through the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office?
sections.html:
Cuyahoga County's Fiscal Officer took over the work of three offices that were once separate: auditor, recorder and engineer. A deed needs one of two forms: the DTE 100 statement of value, or the DTE 100 EX when an exemption from the conveyance fee applies. The county's standards say a standard instrument normally takes three business days to review and must list the parcel number and site address.

  • Recording: $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after, effective October 24, 2024 under Senate Bill 94.
  • Transfer tax: a county may levy up to thirty cents per hundred dollars (Ohio Revised Code 322.02), paid by the grantor before recording.
  • Rate: the closing agent can quote the conveyance amount Cuyahoga County charges on your sale price.

The division answers at 216-443-2060. Heirs can read its Great Estates Program for ways to avoid delay and cost, and owners can sign up for Property Alerts about suspicious filings against their parcel.

sections.h2: Which Strongsville sellers are exempt from the Ohio disclosure form?
sections.html:
The state form under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 has exemptions. Anyone who inherited the house and skipped living in it during the prior year is excused, and so are estate fiduciaries, transfers to a spouse or lineal relative, foreclosures and court-ordered sales.

A covered seller owes every buyer a signed copy promptly. A buyer who receives it only after a contract exists may rescind in writing within three business days, and no later than 30 days after acceptance or the closing.

faqs.q: Does Strongsville require a point-of-sale inspection?
faqs.a: The department describes permit inspections and summer property maintenance checks. Call 440-580-3105 to ask what applies to your address and whether any permits are still open.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Cuyahoga County?
faqs.a: The county's fee is $39 for the first two pages, then $8 for every page after. That schedule began October 24, 2024. Conveyance charges are separate, so request that figure when you book the closing.

faqs.q: Who pays the Cuyahoga County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The grantor, which means you as the seller. The statute sets the ceiling at thirty cents per hundred dollars, and the county decides what it actually levies.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Strongsville house I inherited?
faqs.a: Yes, after whoever holds legal authority signs the deed. The county's Great Estates Program covers ways to avoid delay in settling an estate.

faqs.q: Do I need a contractor to fix permit problems before selling?
faqs.a: Not always. A homeowner permit exists for work you do yourself at your own residence, but any portion handled by a contractor needs one who has registered with the city.
